subtitle: Practice coaching conversations that help colleagues grow: telling coaching apart from correction, using a five-step format, listening and asking open questions, and checking that you offer coaching fairly.
audience: For first-year and experienced supervisors, leads and anyone who helps colleagues develop, including people who coach without supervising. No earlier coaching training is needed.

lessons.title: What coaching is, and what it is not
objectives: Distinguish coaching from directing, correcting and formal performance processes.
Explain why coaching depends on voluntary participation and a shared-learning mindset.
Identify whether an issue affects results or reflects a style you happen to prefer.
Draft one sentence you can use to say which kind of conversation you are starting.
lessons.teaching:
Coaching helps a person build their own ability to do the work. FEMA's leadership course, IS-240 Leadership and Influence, describes a coaching leader as someone who trusts that people will do well with the right training and support. That leader offers support, encouragement and constructive feedback while the person carries the work. Coaching is one of several conversations a leader holds. Directing says what needs to happen and by when. Correcting names a problem with the work and what must change. Formal performance concerns and discipline follow agency procedures, with supervisors, Human Resources and labor relations carrying out their respective responsibilities.

Coaching works best when the person chooses to take part. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2018 memo on coaching says coaching is for learning and development and needs the voluntary participation of the person coached. It adds that coaching should not be a mandatory requirement for poor performance or a stand-in for a supervisor's performance management duties. That is federal guidance, not Minnesota policy. This course uses that distinction as a learning approach. Explain any actual performance concern plainly instead of presenting it as an optional development conversation.

Say which conversation you are starting. A sentence such as "I'd like to talk about how you want to grow in this work, and this isn't about a performance concern" clarifies the purpose, provided it accurately describes the situation. If it is a correction, say that too, kindly and plainly. Then hold the conversation with a shared-learning mindset, which FEMA's format names as part of setting the stage. Give full attention, invite dialogue and expect to learn something yourself. You may know more about the task. You do not know how the work looks from their seat, or what barrier they have already met.

Ask what you treat as the normal way to do the work. A concern described as a skill gap may involve work requirements, an access barrier, a difference in style or several of these. Someone writes longer reports, speaks less in meetings, asks more questions or reaches the answer by a different route. Before you coach, ask whether the issue affects results for people served or for colleagues. Or is it a way of working you learned and happen to prefer? Then notice a second pattern on your team: who usually hears "let's talk it through," and who usually hears "this needs fixing." The last lesson returns to that question.
lessons.keyPoint: Coaching builds a person's own ability, and it works best when they choose to take part. Name the conversation you are having, and check whether the issue is about results or about a style you prefer.
lessons.example: Practice case: Rosalind supervises licensors in disability services. Tobias, a licensor for two years, writes inspection reports that are accurate but long, and two providers have asked for a shorter summary at the top. Rosalind's own reports are brief, a style she learned from her first supervisor. Her manager asks her to "coach Tobias on his writing" before his annual review next month. Tobias has said he wants to take on more complex licensing work.
lessons.question: What should Rosalind do next?
choices: Send Tobias two of her own recent reports as models, and ask him to match their length and layout in his reports from now on.
Offer a coaching talk on the providers' request and his career goal, ask how he writes reports, and keep it apart from the review.
Note the report length for the annual review so the issue is raised formally, fairly and in one place, with time to improve after.
feedback: Models can help, but this treats her own style as the standard and skips his view. He may copy the length without learning what providers need.

This ties the conversation to a real need, connects it to his own goal and keeps coaching apart from the review. Explain the boundaries accurately without promising confidentiality that a supervisor cannot provide.
Using the review keeps things formal, but it turns a growth topic into a performance concern and gives Tobias no chance to work on it first.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time someone coached you well. What did they do that made it feel like growth rather than correction, and do you offer that to others?
lessons.action: Before your next one-to-one, write one sentence you can use to say which kind of conversation you are starting: coaching, direction or correction. Use it, and notice whether the conversation goes differently.

check.question: A manager wants coaching to fix a performance concern before a review. Which approach fits coaching?
check.correct: Offer coaching on a growth goal they choose, and raise the concern separately and plainly.
wrong: Require coaching sessions as the formal step for improving the performance concern.
Use informal coaching chats in place of naming the performance concern directly.
check.feedback: OPM describes coaching as a learning and development activity that needs voluntary participation. It is not a requirement for poor performance and does not replace a supervisor's performance management duties. This is federal guidance used here for the concept.

lessons.title: A five-step coaching conversation
objectives: Apply a five-step coaching format, adapted from FEMA's IS-240, to a real development goal.
Describe how to define an issue together before anyone offers a solution.
Explain how putting inquiry before advocacy keeps options open.
Draft an action plan and follow-up date that the other person helps write.
lessons.teaching:
A simple format makes coaching easier to hold. The format here is adapted from the coaching steps in FEMA's IS-240 Leadership and Influence materials, which begin by setting the stage. This version has five steps: define the issue together, create a growth atmosphere, explore options together, agree on a plan, and follow up. FEMA wrote it for emergency management. The workplace examples here are program adaptations for human services, not tested evidence that this format fits every situation. Required procedures still apply. You will not always move through the steps in order, and that is fine.

Define the issue together before anyone offers a fix. FEMA's format asks the coach to be specific and clear about their own assumptions. Say what you have noticed and why it matters for the work, then ask how the other person sees it. The issue may turn out to be different from what you thought. A program consultant who seems slow to answer lead agencies may be waiting on guidance that never came. Put the goal in terms of the work, such as "lead agencies get a clear answer within the week," rather than "be more responsive."

Create a growth atmosphere, then explore options together. Point to what is already working, say plainly that you are there to help, and invite ideas. FEMA's materials describe a balance between inquiry and advocacy. Inquiry means learning how the other person sees things without judging or arguing. Advocacy means offering your own view and the reasons behind it. FEMA's advice is inquiry first, then advocacy, and to stay open when your ideas are questioned. Let the other person name some of the options. Your ideas are welcome, but offer them as options rather than as the answer.

Agree on a plan, set a follow-up date and keep the door open. A good plan names one or two steps, the support you will give and when you will talk again. Invite the person to summarize the plan in the format that works for them, and agree on what each of you will keep. Follow applicable records requirements; a development conversation does not create a promise of secrecy. At the follow-up, ask what happened, what helped and what got in the way, including anything you did or did not do. Then decide together what to keep, change or stop. When the person asks you to just give them the answer, you can share your view and still ask what they think first.
lessons.keyPoint: Define the issue together, build a climate where ideas are safe, explore options by listening before advising, agree on a short plan the person owns, and follow up on the date you set.
lessons.example: Practice case: Desmond supervises waiver program consultants in the division. Amara joined from a lead agency eight months ago and has asked to lead the next training for county case managers. She has not presented to a large group before, and Desmond noticed her slides for a small meeting were crowded. When they meet, she says, "Just tell me what to fix." The training is in six weeks, and his calendar is full.
lessons.question: What should Desmond do next?
choices: Tell her the three changes he would make to the slides, since she asked directly and the training date is close.
Suggest she co-present this time with an experienced colleague and lead the following session, so the training is safe.
Agree the goal with her, share what he noticed, ask what case managers need, and set a practice run and a date.
feedback: This answers her request and saves time today, but it does not explore her goal, her view of the audience or the support she wants. Specific advice can still be part of coaching after that discussion.
Pairing can be good support, but deciding it for her quietly lowers her goal. Offer it as one option she can weigh, not the plan.
This respects her ask by sharing his view, keeps her thinking about the audience and builds in practice and follow-up within the six weeks.
lessons.reflection: When someone asks you to just tell them the answer, what do you usually do, and what does that choice teach them about their own judgment?
lessons.action: Pick one development goal someone has raised with you. Plan a conversation using the five steps, write two open questions for the first step, and set the follow-up date before the conversation ends.

check.question: In the five-step format adapted from FEMA, what should happen before options are explored?
check.correct: The issue is defined together, and the coach makes clear they are there to help.
wrong: The coach explains the best solution so the person has a clear standard to aim for.
The person drafts an action plan and follow-up date for the coach to approve.
check.feedback: In the format, the issue is defined together and a growth atmosphere is built before options are explored. Explaining the solution first skips the person's own thinking, and the action plan comes after options, not before.

lessons.title: Listening and questions that help someone think
objectives: Use empathic listening and paraphrasing, as described in FEMA's IS-242, to confirm what a person means.
Distinguish open questions that widen thinking from questions that steer toward your answer.
Describe how a coaching habit looks at three points on the intercultural development continuum.
Plan one change to how you invite someone's view when their communication style differs from yours.
lessons.teaching:
Listening helps a coach understand the question before deciding what information or advice may help. FEMA's IS-242 Effective Communication course describes empathic listening as attending to thoughts, beliefs and feelings, not only to words. It describes paraphrasing as restating the main points in your own words, so the speaker can tell whether the message landed. FEMA suggests a paraphrase stay neutral, neither agreeing nor disagreeing. It also lists roadblocks to watch for in yourself, including hearing what you expect instead of what is said, hearing facts but not feelings, and stereotyping.

Open questions widen the other person's thinking. "What have you tried so far?" "What would a good result look like for the family?" "What would make this easier?" Each invites the person to reason. "Have you thought about calling the county?" is advice with a question mark at the end. It has its place, but use it after the person has had room to think. Ask one question at a time. Then leave a silence and let it do some work.

People may think aloud, prefer time to write, or hesitate to disagree with someone who supervises their work. Those observations do not establish capability or explain why a particular person responds that way. The following program illustrations borrow vocabulary from IDI, LLC’s intercultural development continuum to compare coaching approaches. They do not establish a person’s orientation. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I coach everyone the same way, the way that worked for me. An Acceptance habit notices that quick, direct questions suit some people and quiet others. An Adaptation habit changes the conversation, such as sending questions ahead, offering a written option or asking how the person likes to work through a problem. Use these examples to examine your approach, not to label a colleague.

Check whether your adaptation worked. At the end of a conversation, ask what was useful and what would make the next one easier. Notice whether the other person's ideas, not only yours, ended up in the plan. Never guess at someone's background or explain a style by culture. Ask how they like to work, and take the answer at face value. If a colleague mentions a non-visible disability, such as a hearing or processing difference, ask what helps. If they ask for a change at work because of a disability, treat that as an accommodation request: follow the agency's accommodation process with Human Resources or the ADA coordinator, and tell the person who decides. Look at your own defaults too. The style you treat as confident or capable was learned somewhere, and it shapes whom you see as ready.
lessons.keyPoint: Listen for meaning and feeling, paraphrase neutrally and ask open questions before you advise. When styles differ, change how you invite someone's thinking, then ask whether the change helped.
lessons.example: Practice case: Farah supervises an economic assistance policy unit. In weekly check-ins with Joaquin, a newer analyst, she asks quick questions, and he gives short answers and agrees with her suggestions. Later his written notes show careful alternatives he never raised aloud. A peer tells Farah that Joaquin "just needs to speak up" if he wants to grow. Joaquin has asked to work on a policy change that will need briefings with partners.
lessons.question: What should Farah do next?
choices: Ask Joaquin how he likes to work through a problem, send her questions a day ahead, and start the next check-in from his notes.
Coach Joaquin directly on speaking up in check-ins, since voicing ideas aloud will matter in the partner briefings he wants to lead.
Move their check-ins to email for now, since he seems to do his best thinking in writing, and revisit the format in a few months.
feedback: This adapts the conversation so his thinking reaches the plan, and it asks him rather than guessing. Briefing skills can then be a goal they agree together.
Briefing skills may well be worth building, but starting there treats her own style as the standard and loses the ideas he already has.
Writing may suit him, but switching without asking is still a guess, and it removes the spoken practice his briefing goal will need.
lessons.reflection: What communication style did you learn to see as confident or capable, and where did you learn it? How might that shape whom you see as ready?
lessons.action: In your next coaching conversation, try a neutral paraphrase and check that you understood before offering advice. At the end, ask what would make the next conversation easier for the other person, and agree on a useful change within your role, following the accommodation process when it applies.

check.question: Which response is a neutral paraphrase, as FEMA's IS-242 describes it?
check.correct: So the county's change caught you off guard, and you're unsure which guidance to follow.
wrong: You're right, the county should have told you before they changed that guidance.
Have you thought about calling the county to ask what they meant by the change?
check.feedback: A neutral paraphrase restates the main point and the feeling in your own words without agreeing or disagreeing. Taking sides closes the conversation, and a suggestion phrased as a question is still advice.

lessons.title: Coaching fairly and knowing when to hand off
objectives: Explain how patterns in who gets coaching and who gets correction can shape opportunity on a team.
Describe how to help someone draw lessons from a setback without blame.
Distinguish coaching matters from those that belong with Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office.
Plan a private review of your own coaching habits that names no individuals.
lessons.teaching:
Who gets coached and who gets corrected is a pattern worth checking. Coaching is an investment of time, patience and the benefit of the doubt. Different responses to similar work can affect access to development. Compare the work requirements, support offered and relevant circumstances before deciding whether the difference is justified. Familiarity may influence a judgment, but an uneven response alone does not establish why it happened. Direction and development can both be appropriate; the question is whether people have fair access to support.

For this private learning reflection, compare your responses to similar work without putting names or personnel details in the exercise. The reflection does not replace records required by your role. Consider the work standard, circumstances and support offered, then ask whether the differences in your response have a relevant basis. When access to development is uneven, offer a predictable opportunity for coaching with support suited to the person’s goal. An opening question such as “What happened, and what support would help?” can invite useful information without replacing an urgent instruction or required report.

A person may choose to examine a setback as part of a development conversation. The Center for Creative Leadership's early research found that hardships were among the experiences leaders learned from. A 2020 CCL article reports that they were later dropped from the popular 70-20-10 guideline because organizations had little control over them. Treat it as a pointer from leadership research, not a rule. After a setback, ask what happened, what the person would do again, what they would do differently and what support was missing, including from you. Focus on the work and support they want to discuss; do not require personal hardship disclosure or repeated retelling as a condition of development.

Some matters are not coaching matters. OPM's 2018 memo says coaching should not stand in for a supervisor's performance management duties. Consult Human Resources about performance responsibilities when needed; coaching is not a prerequisite for following a required procedure. Bring conduct, discipline and labor agreement questions to Human Resources and labor relations. Follow DHS complaint reporting procedures for discrimination, harassment or retaliation. Supervisors have additional immediate reporting and referral duties; do not wait for a coaching conversation to establish whether the concern is valid. Forward accommodation requests promptly under the agency's accommodation process, and tell the person who decides. Tell the person plainly that this part is now a different conversation. You can keep coaching on other goals.
lessons.keyPoint: Check access to coaching and the reasons for different responses to similar work. Offer fair opportunities with support suited to the person and goal. Follow required reporting and formal procedures without waiting for coaching to resolve the concern.
lessons.example: Practice case: Beatriz, who is blind and uses a screen reader, supervises a provider relations team in the division. This quarter, Abdi and Colin each missed a deadline on a provider enrollment issue. She has known Abdi since they shared a team years ago and talked him through it over coffee. For Colin, she sent an email restating the deadline rules. Rereading her messages, she notices the difference. Colin has since told her his workload doubled after a reassignment, and he asked whether he is being singled out.
lessons.question: What should Beatriz do next?
choices: Apologize to Colin for the uneven response, offer him the same coaching conversation Abdi had, and adjust his workload herself right away.
Offer Colin the same coaching talk, ask about the workload change, use one approach for missed deadlines and say where fairness concerns go.
Ask Human Resources to review the situation before she speaks with Colin again, so that she does not make his concern any worse by accident.
feedback: Owning the difference matters, but changing his workload before asking what changed is still deciding for him, and his question about fair treatment needs a clear route.

This repairs the coaching gap, looks at the workload, changes her method and explains the applicable route for a fairness concern. If the information triggers a reporting duty, the supervisor must follow it and explain that responsibility.
Seeking advice is wise, but going silent while she waits leaves Colin without support and may feel like the very pattern he asked about.
lessons.reflection: When work goes wrong on your team, what is your first sentence? Would it sound the same whoever had made the mistake?
lessons.action: This week, offer each person you supervise or support the same chance at a coaching conversation on a goal they choose. Hold the first one with the five steps, send questions ahead and set a follow-up date before you finish.

check.question: Which situation should a supervisor stop coaching on and bring to Human Resources or another responsible partner?
check.correct: An employee says a coworker's repeated comments about her religion make work hard.
wrong: An employee wants to get better at leading meetings with lead agency partners.
An employee asks for help recovering from a report that went out with errors.
check.feedback: Repeated comments about religion may be harassment, which goes promptly to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office. Building meeting skills and learning from a mistake are ordinary coaching goals.

cards.back: A conversation that helps a person build their own ability to do the work, offered for learning and development and taken up by choice.
A conversation that names a problem with the work and what must change. It is honest and needed at times, but it is not coaching.
Coming to a coaching conversation expecting to learn as well as help, with full attention, open dialogue and mutual respect.
Learning how the other person sees an issue, without judging or arguing, before offering your own view and the reasons for it.
Restating someone's main point and feeling in your own words, without agreeing or disagreeing, so they can tell whether you understood.

aid.heading: Before a coaching conversation
items: Decide whether this is coaching, direction or correction, and plan how you will say so.
Ask whether the issue affects results or reflects a style you happen to prefer.
Send your opening questions ahead so the person can think or write first.
Check privately whom you have offered coaching to lately, without naming anyone in notes.

aid.heading: The five steps, in the conversation
items: Define the issue together, starting with what each of you has noticed.
Create a growth atmosphere: name what is working and say you are there to help.
Explore options together, listening and paraphrasing before you advise.
Agree on one or two steps, the support you will give and a follow-up date.
Follow up on the date, ask what helped, and decide together what to keep, change or stop.

aid.heading: When it is no longer a coaching matter
items: Consult Human Resources about performance responsibilities when needed; coaching is not a prerequisite for required procedures.
Bring conduct, discipline and labor agreement questions to Human Resources and labor relations.
Follow designated complaint reporting procedures promptly, including supervisors’ additional immediate reporting and referral duties.
Forward accommodation requests promptly under the agency's accommodation process, and tell the person who decides.
Tell the person plainly that this part is now a different conversation.

sources.note: Supports the lesson 4 statements that CCL's early research found leaders learning from hardships, and that hardships were later dropped from the 70-20-10 guideline because organizations had little control over them. A 2020 practitioner article.

sources.note: Supports complaint reporting and supervisors’ added referral duties. The public copy uses an earlier division name; confirm current contacts and procedures on the DHS intranet.

sources.note: Supports supervisors’ immediate report to Human Resources or the agency affirmative action officer under agency procedures.
